wine.name: Mantinia
wine.grapes: Moschofilero alone, the pink skinned grape of the plateau.
wine.sites: Selected vineyards around the villages of Rizes, Lithovounia and Agiorgitika, at about 680 metres on the south eastern side of the Mantinia plateau, below the foothills of Mount Parnon.
wine.making: The grapes are given a short cold soak on their skins, about eight hours at 10 degrees Celsius, before a slow, cool fermentation. The wine then rests only briefly in stainless steel tanks on its fine lees before it is bottled young, with no oak.
wine.glass: Fresh lemon and rose petal, delicate in weight yet intense in scent; light in body and low in alcohol, with high, bright acidity and a clean, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first two or three years, while the perfume is fresh; a good vintage holds a little longer.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of modest size.

records.table: Domaine Tselepos makes its Mantinia from Moschofilero grown at Rizes and two neighbouring villages, high on the Arcadian plateau. Given a few hours on the skins and bottled young from steel, it smells of rose and lemon and drinks light, dry and bright.
records.story: An oenologist trained in Dijon settled on the Mantinia plateau in 1981, an appellation drawn up only ten years before, and worked first as a consultant to local wineries. In 1989, by the house's own account, he and his wife founded their own estate outside the village of Rizes, on the clay hills at the foot of Mount Parnon, at the south eastern edge of the plateau. Their first Mantinia under the family name followed within a year or two, Moschofilero bottled alone. The estate's own timeline then runs on through a red blend in 1993, its own winery opened in 1994, and in 1996 Amalia Brut, a sparkling Moschofilero made by the traditional method of Champagne, which the house counts as the first sparkling Moschofilero made that way. In 2003 the family bought Driopi, an estate in Nemea, and it later joined the Chryssou family's Canava on Santorini, so its three wineries stand in three Greek appellations. Through all of it the Mantinia has stayed the house's calling card: Moschofilero picked late on the cold plateau and bottled as a pure, fresh dry white. Here is what the appellation is meant to be: perfume, freshness and low alcohol from a cold, high place.

records.table: Around Artemisio, Domaine Spiropoulos, one of the plateau's old families and an early organic grower, ferments the Moschofilero of its Mantinia cool in steel. Orange blossom and rose lead a slight, dry white that opens a meal well.
records.story: The Spiropoulos family has tended vines on the Mantinia plateau since 1860, by its own account, near the ruins of ancient Mantineia in the heart of Arcadia. The modern estate took shape when, as the house's page tells it, the family began building a new winery in 1989 to a design of 1987, built around a traditional Arcadian stone tower, and from it bottled Moschofilero under its own name in the Mantinia appellation, drawn up in 1971. The family turned early to organic farming: by the account of Wines of Greece its vineyards met the European organic rules from 1993 and were certified by the Greek body DIO in 1996. The family also grows red Agiorgitiko on a second estate in Nemea, where it built a second winery, and it makes a sparkling Mantinia, Ode Panos, beside its still one. The Mantinia remains the wine the house is known by: organic Moschofilero from three zones of the plateau, fermented cool and bottled young. It is the appellation's traditional, unadorned face, and the bottle to reach for when a guest asks for an organic Greek white.

wine.name: Holy Mania
wine.sites: The family's own low yielding vineyards in the Fteri area at the centre of the plateau, at about 640 metres.
wine.making: The house works with as little intervention and as few additions as it can: the Moschofilero is fermented wild, with the yeasts of the vineyard and cellar rather than a chosen strain, and the wine is bottled young.
wine.glass: White peach and citron on the nose and a note of jasmine on the finish; dry and fresh, with lively acidity and a fuller flavour on the palate than its scent suggests.
wine.ageing: Drinks well on release and keeps for at least three years, by the house's account.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

records.table: Holy Mania is the Mantinia of Troupis, a family winery at Fteri in the centre of the plateau: Moschofilero from its own vines, fermented with wild yeasts. White peach, citron and jasmine, dry and fresh; serve it cool, not icy.
records.story: From the 1970s on, the Troupis family has worked the land of the Mantinia plateau, an appellation since 1971, growing vines and fruit and, by its own account, making wine for the household each year and selling the rest of its grapes. In 2010 the family chose to build on its own vineyards rather than sell their fruit, and the winery was set up at Fteri, in the middle of the plateau at about 700 metres. The same year it launched its first labels under the name of the village, Fteri, and its first exports were Fteri Moschofilero, a wine labelled PGI Arcadia. The winery has kept planting its own vines year by year and has trialled Moschofilero on different rootstocks, along with small batches of forgotten local grapes such as Kolliniatiko. Holy Mania is one of its two Mantinia wines, beside Tomi: Moschofilero from the family's own vines around Fteri, fermented wild with the yeasts of the place. Beside it the house makes Hoof and Lur, a skin contact Moschofilero, and a sweet wine. The house is the plateau's younger generation in miniature: small, family run, curious, and built on the one local grape.

records.table: At Steno, on the Mantinia plateau, the Bosinakis family works with Moschofilero alone, and its Mantinia, first bottled under the family's label in 2009, comes from dry farmed vines at about 700 metres. Rose, lemon and white pepper sit on a lean, lively frame.
records.story: The Bosinakis family's winery at Steno, a village of the Mantinia plateau near Tripoli, began making wine in 1992, and for its first years it did not bottle under its own name. That changed in 2009, when a brother and sister of the family released their first wine under the Bosinakis label, a Mantinia from Moschofilero. The family's vines lie around Steno and the neighbouring villages of Lithovounia and Agiorgitika, on clay loam at about 700 metres, and they are dry farmed, as the cold, wet winters of the plateau allow. The range has since grown by small steps, all of it from the one grape: a rosé, Iereia, from the pink skins of Moschofilero, and an orange wine, Aspela, given long contact with its skins. The family's line runs back beyond the winery, but the sources disagree on how far, and the record does not guess. Mantinia's wine was already sent to Athens in the nineteenth century, by the account of Wines of Greece; houses like this one bottle it at the village. Bosinakis gives the appellation from one family's vines, a small house known at home and in a few export markets.

records.table: Semeli Mantinia Nassiakos is the Moschofilero of a house better known for Nemea, made at its Nassiakos winery in Mantinia from vines at Zevgolatio. Fermented slowly in steel, it gives lemon and rose petal and a brisk, featherweight finish.
records.story: Semeli began in 1979 at Stamata, in the hills of Attica north of Athens, where its first winery was built, and it took its name from Semele, the mother of Dionysus in Greek myth. From there the company bought vineyards in the Peloponnese, in Nemea and on the Mantinia plateau. In 2003 it opened a large modern winery at Koutsi, at about 600 metres in Nemea, among its own vines, and that cellar became the heart of the house, making the house's Agiorgitiko. Its third winery is in Mantinia: the Nassiakos winery, a cellar with, by the house's account, some forty years of making Moschofilero behind it. The house's Mantinia carries that cellar's name, Nassiakos, on its label, and comes from Moschofilero grown at Zevgolatio at about 650 metres, fermented slowly and cool. A house whose reds come from Nemea and whose white comes from the plateau above Tripoli holds the two Peloponnese appellations a candidate meets most often under one name. The wine shows how a larger house keeps a cellar of its own on the plateau for its Moschofilero.
